title: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science

learn.hook: Why does the dosa batter rise overnight in summer but stay flat in a cold Delhi winter? Asking 'why' and then testing the answer is exactly how science works.
points: Science starts with careful observation and a question that can be tested.
A hypothesis is a possible, testable explanation, for example 'warm batter ferments faster than cold batter'.
A fair test changes only one thing (the independent variable), measures one result (the dependent variable) and keeps everything else the same (controlled variables).
Repeating an experiment and comparing results makes the conclusion more reliable.
If the evidence does not support the hypothesis, scientists change the hypothesis and test again. Results are shared so others can check them.

example.q: Think it through: Meera wants to know if salt dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water. How should she plan a fair test?
steps: Change only one thing: the temperature of the water (hot and cold).
Measure one result: the time taken for the salt to dissolve completely.
Keep the same amount of water, the same amount of salt, the same kind of glass and the same stirring.
Repeat each trial a few times and compare the average times. Use warm tap water, not boiling water, and ask an adult to help.
example.answer: Vary only the water temperature, time the dissolving, keep all else the same and repeat the trials.

learn.reallife: Doctors testing a new medicine, farmers comparing two fertilisers on equal plots and ISRO engineers testing rocket parts all use fair tests.

games.title: Steps of a scientific investigation
games.prompt: Arrange the usual steps of an investigation from first to last
items: Observe something puzzling
Ask a testable question
Form a hypothesis
Test it with a fair experiment
Analyse the data
Draw a conclusion and share it

games.title: Observation or inference?
items: The leaves of the money plant are yellow
The thermometer reads 38 °C
The ice cube melted in 10 minutes
The puddle is smaller in the evening than in the morning
The plant is yellow because it got too little water
Someone must have left the fridge door open
The dog barked because it saw a stranger
The puddle shrank because the Sun heated it

quiz.q: Arjun says, "Tulsi plants kept in sunlight will grow taller than tulsi plants kept in shade." What is this statement?
quiz.explain: It is a possible explanation that can be tested by an experiment, so it is a hypothesis. It becomes a conclusion only after the evidence is collected.
steps: The statement is a possible explanation about sunlight and growth.
It can be tested by growing plants in sun and in shade.
A possible, testable explanation is a hypothesis.
It is not yet a conclusion, as no evidence has been collected.
Answer: A hypothesis
quiz.mistake: Confuses a prediction made before testing with a conclusion drawn after testing

quiz.q: Priya tests how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls. What is the dependent variable?
options: The mass of the toy car
quiz.explain: The dependent variable is the result you measure. Priya changes the ramp height and measures the distance rolled.
steps: Independent variable = what is changed: ramp height.
Dependent variable = the result measured.
Priya measures how far the car rolls.
Answer: The distance the car rolls
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the variable that is changed (independent) with the one that is measured (dependent)

quiz.q: To test whether more water makes moong seedlings grow faster, which of these must be kept the same for all pots?
options: The number of leaves that grow
The amount of sunlight each pot gets
quiz.explain: Sunlight is a controlled variable: if it differs, you cannot tell whether water or light caused the change. Water is the variable being changed, while height and number of leaves are results that are measured.
steps: Changed (independent): amount of water.
Measured (dependent): height, number of leaves.
Everything else must be controlled, e.g. sunlight.
Answer: The amount of sunlight each pot gets
quiz.mistake: Thinks the variable being tested should also be kept constant

quiz.q: Why do scientists repeat an experiment several times?
options: To change the hypothesis every time
To make the experiment take longer
To make the results reliable and spot errors
To use up all the materials
quiz.explain: Repeating trials shows whether the results are consistent and reduces the effect of chance errors.
steps: One trial can be affected by chance errors.
Repeating and comparing shows whether results are consistent.
This makes the conclusion more reliable.
Answer: To make the results reliable and spot errors
quiz.mistake: Does not see why one single trial may give a misleading result

quiz.q: The results of Kabir's experiment do not support his hypothesis. What should he do?
options: Change the data so it fits
Revise the hypothesis and test again
Report that the hypothesis was proved
quiz.explain: Evidence decides. A hypothesis that does not fit the data is revised or replaced and then tested again. Data must never be changed to fit an idea.
steps: Evidence decides whether a hypothesis stands.
If the data do not support it, change the hypothesis.
Then test again; never alter data to fit.
Answer: Revise the hypothesis and test again
quiz.mistake: Believes a hypothesis must be right and that disagreeing data is a failure

quiz.q: Which of these questions can be answered by a scientific experiment?
options: Does sugar dissolve faster in warm water than in cold water?
Is the rose the most beautiful flower?
Which festival is the most fun?
Is blue a nicer colour than green?
quiz.explain: Dissolving time can be measured and compared. The other questions are matters of personal opinion and cannot be measured.
steps: A scientific question must be testable and measurable.
Dissolving time in warm vs cold water can be measured.
Beauty, fun and nicer colour are opinions.
Answer: Does sugar dissolve faster in warm water than in cold water?
quiz.mistake: Does not separate measurable questions from questions of opinion

quiz.q: Which statement is an observation rather than an inference?
options: Someone forgot to boil the milk
The milk was left out too long
quiz.explain: A smell is noticed directly with the senses, so it is an observation. The other options are explanations we guess from it.
steps: An observation is noticed directly with the senses.
'The milk smells sour' is sensed directly.
Bacteria, forgetting to boil, or time left out are inferred explanations.
Answer: The milk smells sour
quiz.mistake: Treats an explanation for what was seen as the observation itself

quiz.q: National Science Day is celebrated in India on 28 February. Which discovery does it mark?
quiz.explain: C.V. Raman announced the Raman effect, about how light is scattered, on 28 February 1928. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
steps: 28 February is National Science Day in India.
It marks C.V. Raman's announcement of the Raman effect (1928).
Answer: The Raman effect
quiz.mistake: Links the day to a famous space mission or another well-known discovery

teach.ask: Gappu flutters about: "I think birds sing more when it rains! How would a scientist check if I am right?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Make a testable guess, change one thing at a time, measure, repeat and let the evidence decide. I am going to count bird songs tomorrow!
teach.nudge: But if I change lots of things at the same time, how will I know which one made the difference?

revise.summary: Science starts with observation and a testable question. A hypothesis is tested by a fair test that changes one variable, measures one result and controls the rest, and is revised if evidence disagrees.
focus: Independent, dependent and controlled variables in a fair test
What to do when evidence does not support a hypothesis
remember: Independent = changed; dependent = measured; controlled = kept the same
traps: Don't confuse the variable you change with the result you measure
Never change data to fit a hypothesis
An inference (explanation) is not an observation

learn.hook: Nobody has seen an atom with their eyes, yet scientists can predict how atoms behave. How? They build models!
points: A scientific model is a simplified picture of something real: a physical model (a globe), a diagram (a drawing of a cell), a mathematical model (an equation) or a computer model.
Models help us explain what we see and predict what will happen next.
A good model makes predictions that can be tested by observation or experiment.
Every model has limits. A globe shows the shape of the continents but not the height of every hill.
When new evidence disagrees with a model, the model is improved or replaced, as happened with the models of the atom.

example.q: Think it through: A model says the Moon shines only because it reflects sunlight. What does this model predict will happen when the Earth comes exactly between the Sun and the Moon?
steps: If moonlight is reflected sunlight, the Moon needs sunlight to reach it.
When the Earth is exactly in between, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
So less sunlight reaches the Moon and it should look dim.
This is what we see in a lunar eclipse, so the observation supports the model.
example.answer: The Moon should become dim, which is what happens during a lunar eclipse.

learn.reallife: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) uses computer models of the atmosphere to forecast the monsoon and warn people about cyclones.

games.title: Match the model to what it represents
pairs: A labelled drawing of a leaf cell

games.title: True or false: models
items: A model can be useful even though it is simpler than the real thing
Models leave out details on purpose so that the main idea is easy to understand and use.
Once a scientific model is accepted, it can never be changed
Models are revised when new evidence disagrees with them, like the models of the atom.
An equation can be a scientific model
Mathematical models such as distance = speed × time describe and predict how things behave.
A model that makes no testable predictions is a strong scientific model
A scientific model is valuable because its predictions can be checked against observations.
Weather forecasts are made using computer models of the atmosphere
Forecasters feed measurements into computer models that predict how the weather will change.

quiz.q: Why is a globe called a model of the Earth?
options: It is exactly the same size as the Earth
It shows every road and building
It is a smaller, simplified copy that shows the Earth's main features
It is made of the same rocks as the Earth
quiz.explain: A model is a simplified representation. A globe keeps the shape and positions of continents and oceans but leaves out most details.
steps: A model is a simplified picture of something real.
A globe is a small copy showing continents and oceans, leaving out details.
Answer: It is a smaller, simplified copy that shows the Earth's main features
quiz.mistake: Thinks a model must be a perfect, full-detail copy

quiz.q: What makes a scientific model useful?
options: It explains observations and makes predictions that can be tested
quiz.explain: A model earns trust when its predictions match observations. Testable predictions are its main strength.
steps: Models help explain what we see and predict what happens next.
A good model's predictions can be tested.
Answer: It explains observations and makes predictions that can be tested
quiz.mistake: Judges a model by appearance instead of by its predictions

quiz.q: A model predicts that a ball will land 5 m away, but careful repeated measurements show 8 m. What should scientists do?
options: Measure only once more and stop
quiz.explain: When reliable evidence disagrees with a prediction, the model has to be improved or replaced.
steps: Prediction 5 m; repeated careful measurements 8 m.
Reliable evidence disagrees with the model.
So the model must be improved or replaced.
Answer: Improve or replace the model
quiz.mistake: Trusts the model more than repeated careful measurements

quiz.q: Which of these is a mathematical model?
options: A clay model of a volcano
A chart drawing of the heart
quiz.explain: A mathematical model uses an equation to describe and predict. The other three are physical models or diagrams.
steps: Types: physical model, diagram, mathematical model (equation), computer model.
distance = speed × time is an equation.
Answer: The formula distance = speed × time
quiz.mistake: Thinks only objects you can hold count as models

quiz.q: A school chart shows the Sun and planets in a row on one sheet. What is a limitation of this model?
options: It shows the order of the planets
Its sizes and distances are not to scale
quiz.explain: Real distances between planets are enormous compared with their sizes, so a chart cannot show both to scale on one sheet.
steps: Every model has limits.
Planet distances are huge compared with their sizes.
One sheet cannot show both to scale.
Answer: Its sizes and distances are not to scale
quiz.mistake: Does not realise that every model leaves out or changes something

quiz.q: Which Indian organisation issues official weather forecasts and cyclone warnings using computer models?
quiz.explain: IMD is India's national weather agency. It runs weather models and issues forecasts and warnings.
steps: Weather forecasts use computer models.
India's national weather agency is IMD.
Answer: India Meteorological Department (IMD)
quiz.mistake: Does not know which agency is responsible for weather

quiz.q: Ravi's model says, "Heavier objects sink in water." A large wooden log floats. What does this show?
options: The model is incomplete and needs to be improved
The log is not really heavy
The observation should be thrown away
quiz.explain: A heavy log floating disagrees with the prediction, so the model needs improving. Floating depends on density, not on weight alone.
steps: Prediction: heavier objects sink.
Observation: a heavy log floats.
Evidence disagrees, so the model is incomplete and must be improved.
Answer: The model is incomplete and needs to be improved
quiz.mistake: Rejects an observation instead of questioning the model

quiz.q: Which statement about scientific models is correct?
options: A model must include every detail of the real object
A model is only for small children
A model is the same as a guess with no evidence
A model can be useful even if it is not perfect
quiz.explain: All models simplify. They are useful as long as they explain and predict well enough for their purpose.
steps: Every model simplifies and has limits.
A model is useful if it explains and predicts well enough.
Answer: A model can be useful even if it is not perfect
quiz.mistake: Thinks an imperfect model is useless

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: "My globe is tiny and has no mountains on it. Why do scientists still call it a model of the Earth?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! A model is a simple version that helps us explain and predict, and it can be improved when new evidence comes. My globe is still super useful!
teach.nudge: But what happens if the real world does not do what the model said it would?

revise.summary: A scientific model is a simplified picture of something real: physical, diagram, mathematical or computer. Models explain and predict, have limits, and are improved or replaced when evidence disagrees.
focus: Testable predictions as a model's strength
Improving a model when evidence disagrees
remember: Physical (globe), diagram (cell drawing), mathematical (equation), computer model
A good model makes testable predictions
IMD uses computer models for forecasts
traps: A model need not include every detail to be useful
Don't ignore evidence that disagrees with a model
A model is not an untested guess

learn.hook: How many grains of rice are in a 1 kg packet? You don't need to count them all. A clever estimate gets you close in a minute!
points: Estimation means finding a sensible approximate value using things you know, simple rounding and reasoning.
A good estimate is quick and close enough to judge whether an answer is reasonable.
Scientific notation writes numbers as a × 10ⁿ, where a is at least 1 and less than 10. For example 3,50,000 = 3.5 × 10⁵.
Scientists all over the world use SI units. There are 7 SI base units, including the metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time) and kelvin (temperature).
Always check: is my answer about the right size? A classroom door 20 m tall cannot be right!

example.q: Think it through: About how many grains of rice are in a 1 kg packet, if 100 grains weigh about 2 g?
steps: 100 grains weigh about 2 g, so 1 g has about 50 grains.
Number of grains ≈ 1000 × 50 = 50 000.
In scientific notation that is about 5 × 10⁴ grains.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers estimate stock, cooks estimate rice for a wedding feast and election officials estimate how many voters a booth can handle in a day.

items.text: The SI unit of length is the ___.
The SI unit of mass is the ___.
The SI unit of temperature is the ___.
In scientific notation, 4 000 is written as 4 × ___.

quiz.q: Your stride is about 0.5 m long. Roughly how many steps will you take to walk 1 km?
quiz.explain: 1 km = 1000 m. Number of steps = 1000 ÷ 0.5 = 2000.
steps: Answer: 2000
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert kilometres to metres, or multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q: Which is the best estimate of the height of a classroom door?
quiz.explain: A door is a little taller than an adult, so about 2 m is sensible. 20 m would be as tall as a six-storey building.
steps: An adult is about 1.6–1.8 m tall; a door is a little taller.
So about 2 m is sensible.
20 m and 200 m are far too tall; 0.2 m too short.
Answer: 2 m
quiz.mistake: Has no feel for the size of a metre

quiz.q: If you sleep 8 hours every night, about how many hours do you sleep in a year of 365 days?
quiz.explain: 8 hours × 365 nights = 2920 hours, about one-third of all the hours in a year.
steps: Hours per night = 8
Answer: 2920
quiz.mistake: Makes a place-value slip while multiplying

quiz.q: How is 3 000 000 written in scientific notation?
quiz.explain: Move the decimal point 6 places to get 3. The first number must be at least 1 and less than 10, so it is 3 × 10⁶.
steps: Scientific notation: a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.
3 000 000: move the decimal 6 places left → a = 3.
Answer: 3 × 10⁶
quiz.mistake: Miscounts the zeros or writes a first number that is not between 1 and 10

quiz.q: How many SI base units are there?
quiz.explain: The 7 SI base units are the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
steps: SI base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela.
Count = 7.
Answer: 7
quiz.mistake: Remembers only the common units of length, mass and time

quiz.q: If each person uses about 100 litres of water a day, roughly how much water does a family of 4 use in a week?
quiz.explain: Per day the family uses 100 × 4 = 400 litres. In 7 days that is 400 × 7 = 2800 litres.
steps: 100 × 4 = 400 litres per day
400 × 7 = 2800 litres per week
Answer: 2800 litres
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by only one of the two factors (people or days)

quiz.q: Which number is written correctly in scientific notation?
quiz.explain: All four equal 4500, but only 4.5 × 10³ has a first number that is at least 1 and less than 10.
steps: All four equal 4500.
Rule: the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10.
Only 4.5 lies in that range.
Answer: 4.5 × 10³
quiz.mistake: Thinks any form with a power of 10 is scientific notation

quiz.q: Which is the SI unit of time?
quiz.explain: The second is the SI base unit of time. Minutes, hours and days are commonly used but are not SI base units.
steps: The SI base unit of time is the second.
Minutes, hours and days are not SI base units.
Answer: Second
quiz.mistake: Confuses everyday units with SI base units

teach.ask: Gappu looks at a huge pile of mangoes in the market: "I cannot count them all! How can I know roughly how many there are?"
teach.praise: Wow! Count a small part, multiply up, round the numbers and check that it makes sense. I estimated 600 mangoes in two minutes!
teach.nudge: Okay, but how do I go from counting a small part to the whole pile?

revise.summary: Estimation finds a sensible approximate value by reasoning. Scientific notation writes numbers as a × 10ⁿ with a from 1 to less than 10, and scientists use the 7 SI base units.
focus: Making sensible estimates and checking answer size
remember: 7 SI base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela
traps: 45 × 10² is not correct notation; the first number must be below 10
Minutes and hours are not SI base units
Always check the size: a 20 m door is unreasonable
